sections: Validity in predicate logic means the same as in propositional logic — the conclusion holds whenever the hypotheses do — but the proofs need four extra rules for getting quantifiers off and back on.

An argument in predicate logic is **valid** when there is no **interpretation** — a domain together with meanings for the predicates — making all hypotheses true and the conclusion false.

The four quantifier rules:

| name | from | conclude | condition |
|---|---|---|---|
| Universal instantiation (UI) | $\forall x\,P(x)$ | $P(c)$ | any $c$ |
| Universal generalisation (UG) | $P(c)$ | $\forall x\,P(x)$ | $c$ **arbitrary** |
| Existential instantiation (EI) | $\exists x\,P(x)$ | $P(c)$ | $c$ **new** |
| Existential generalisation (EG) | $P(c)$ | $\exists x\,P(x)$ | any $c$ |

The conditions are not decoration. They are what makes the rules sound.

> "If I work, it is either sunny or partly sunny." "I worked last Friday." "It was not partly sunny on Friday."

Hypotheses: $\forall x\,(W(x) \to (S(x)\vee P(x)))$, $\;W(F)$, $\;\neg P(F)$.

| | | |
|---|---|---|
| (1) | $\forall x (W(x) \to (S(x)\vee P(x)))$ | hyp. |
| (2) | $W(F) \to (S(F) \vee P(F))$ | UI, (1) |
| (3) | $W(F)$ | hyp. |
| (4) | $S(F) \vee P(F)$ | MP, (2), (3) |
| (5) | $\neg P(F)$ | hyp. |
| (6) | $S(F)$ | DS, (4), (5) |

Strip the quantifier, work propositionally, put it back if needed.

**EI must use a fresh constant.** From $\exists x\,P(x)$ and $\exists x\,Q(x)$ you may **not** conclude $P(c) \wedge Q(c)$ — the two witnesses need not be the same object. Using one letter twice is the commonest fatal error in these derivations.

**UG needs the constant to be arbitrary.** If $c$ arrived by EI, or was named in a hypothesis, you may not generalise over it.

**To disprove, give an interpretation.** A counterexample here is a **domain plus predicates**, not a truth assignment. Choosing a tiny domain — one or two elements — usually makes the counterexample obvious.

*"Show the argument is valid"* — a derivation, naming UI/EI/UG/EG as well as the propositional rules.
*"Show it is invalid"* — an interpretation. Name the domain, define each predicate on it, and evaluate every hypothesis and the conclusion.

[Practice Assignment 3, Exercise 17](#PA03-FoL-AIO_ex17) onwards, [Practice Assignment 2, Exercise 6](#PA02-Inferences_ex6) (a predicate-logic derivation in full). Lecture 3 — Predicate Calculus & FoL, Lecture 3 — Predicate Calculus & FoL.

entries.title: Variables and quantification
asks: what is a quantifier
what does for all mean
how do I negate a quantifier
difference between universal and existential
what is a bound variable
the upside down a and the backwards e
saying every and saying at least one
when does a formula with x get a truth value
what does it mean for a variable to be tied down
not everyone becomes someone is not
i dont get why p of x is not true or false
symbol that means there is at least one
how to say every student in symbols
free variable versus one that is captured
quantifiers explained in plain words
sections: $\forall$ says "every", $\exists$ says "at least one", and each **binds** a variable so that the statement finally has a truth value.

Over a domain $D$:

- $\forall x\, P(x)$ is true when $P(a)$ holds for **every** $a \in D$.
- $\exists x\, P(x)$ is true when $P(a)$ holds for **at least one** $a \in D$.

A variable is **bound** when a quantifier governs it, and **free** otherwise. A formula with a free variable is not a proposition in this course.

**The negation rules**, which are used constantly:

$$\neg \forall x\, P(x) \;\equiv\; \exists x\, \neg P(x) \qquad\qquad \neg \exists x\, P(x) \;\equiv\; \forall x\, \neg P(x)$$

In words: the negation moves inward and **flips the quantifier**.

"Every student passed" — $\forall x\, P(x)$. Its negation is **not** "every student failed". It is

$$\exists x\, \neg P(x)$$

"**Some** student did not pass." One is enough. That asymmetry is the whole content of the rules.

**The negation of "all" is "some not", never "none".** $\neg\forall x P(x)$ is $\exists x \neg P(x)$; "none" would be $\forall x \neg P(x)$, which is much stronger. Getting this backwards is the most expensive single error in the chapter, because everything downstream inherits it.

**The shapes of $\forall$ and $\exists$ statements differ.** A universal claim over a conditional is $\forall x\,(S(x) \to P(x))$ — "every student passed". An existential claim uses a **conjunction**: $\exists x\,(S(x) \wedge P(x))$ — "some student passed". Writing $\exists x\,(S(x) \to P(x))$ is a classic error: it is true whenever anything at all is not a student.

**One counterexample disproves a universal claim; no number of examples proves one.** This is a standing ruling of the course and it applies to every $\forall$ statement you meet.

*Translation* into and out of symbols, where the $\to$/$\wedge$ pairing above is the trap.
*Negation* — push $\neg$ all the way inside, flipping every quantifier and finishing with De Morgan on the connectives.
*Truth value over a given domain* — a full answer names the witness for $\exists$, or the counterexample for a false $\forall$.

[Practice Assignment 3, Exercise 3](#PA03-FoL-AIO_ex3) to [Exercise 12](#PA03-FoL-AIO_ex12) (translation and negation), [Exercise 17](#PA03-FoL-AIO_ex17) onwards. Lecture 3 — Predicate Calculus & FoL, Lecture 3 — Predicate Calculus & FoL.

sections: Nearly every question in this course has a **cheap check** that costs seconds and catches the error. Learn the check that goes with each kind of question, and use it every time.

| after you have… | check |
|---|---|
| found $\gcd$ and $\mathrm{lcm}$ | does $\gcd \times \mathrm{lcm} = ab$? |
| found Bézout coefficients $s,t$ | multiply out: is $sa+tb$ really the gcd? |
| solved $ax \equiv b \pmod m$ | substitute your $x$ back |
| computed a remainder | is it in $\{0,\ldots,m-1\}$? |
| listed degrees in a graph | do they sum to $2|E|$ — or, directed, to $|E|$ each way? |
| used Euler's formula | substitute back into $p-q+r=2$ |
| listed a power set | is the count $2^{n}$, and is $\varnothing$ in it? |
| found equivalence classes | do they cover the set and not overlap? |
| written a proof sequence | do all cited line numbers exist and come earlier? |
| written an Euler circuit | is its length the number of edges? |
| solved a system of congruences | is the answer's modulus the lcm of the moduli? |
| counted vertices or edges of $K_n$, $W_n$ | check against the handshaking theorem |

**Two general checks that apply almost everywhere:**

**Does the answer have the right *type*?** A congruence's answer is a class, not a number. A cardinality is a number, not a list. A counterexample is values plus two evaluations. A great many lost marks are a correct calculation of the wrong kind of object.

**Read the question header again.** Second reading, after you think you are finished. It catches the part you answered in the wrong form.
What the course says, and what it does not

These checks come from the course's own worked solutions, which use them — the inclusion–exclusion answer verifies $125 \times 5000 = 625{,}000$; the extended Euclidean answers multiply back out.

**A passing check does not prove your answer is right** — it proves it is not wrong in the one way the check tests. But most errors in this course are arithmetic slips and sign errors, and these checks catch exactly those.

- **Checking nothing** because the working "looked fine".
- **Re-reading your own working** instead of testing the answer independently. You will read what you meant to write.
- **Skipping the check on the easy parts.** That is where confidence makes slips.

entries.title: The common ways to lose marks
asks: why did I lose marks
common mistakes in this course

the five recurring errors in this course

sections:
Almost all of them are **presentation and instruction-reading**, not mathematics. The five that recur:

1. Giving examples where a proof was required.
2. Writing "clearly" or "obviously" instead of an argument.
3. Reaching the right answer without the reasoning.
4. Answering by the wrong method, because the header named one.
5. Giving one solution where the answer is a whole class.

**Examples never prove a universal claim.** The course states it outright: *"Do not give an example, or a million examples, when the required proof contains a universal generalization."* One counterexample **disproves** a universal claim; no number of examples proves one. Students confuse the two constantly, and it is the single most costly habit in the course.

**"Clearly" and "obviously" earn nothing.** If a step is worth stating, it is worth proving. *"Clearly transitive"* is not a proof of transitivity.

**The verdict without the reasoning is not a full answer.** *"In real tests, students must explicitly include all required information."*

**The wrong method scores zero however well executed.** A truth table where the header said "without truth tables"; a membership table where the header said containment only.

**A congruence has a class for an answer, not a number.** $x \equiv 8 \pmod 9$, not $x = 8$. The same applies to any question whose answer is a set: give the set.

And a handful of specific ones, each of which has cost real marks:

- **Reporting a negative remainder.** $-17 \bmod 2 = 1$, never $-1$, whatever your programming language says.
- **Omitting $\varnothing$ from a power set.**
- **Omitting $1$ from a list of numbers relatively prime to $n$.**
- **Forgetting the outer region** when counting faces with Euler's formula.
- **Treating equal degree sequences as proof of isomorphism.** Necessary, never sufficient.
- **Answering "not isomorphic" or "no Hamilton cycle" with no invariant or obstruction named.** Failing to find one is not an argument.
What the course says, and what it does not

Everything above is drawn from the course's own material and rulings, or from the exercises where it is demonstrated. **It is not a list of what your marker deducts for** — the per-question marking breakdowns are not published here.
The whole entry is the list. The one habit that prevents most of it: **read the header, then read your own answer back against it** before moving on.

sections:
A handful of things in this course are settled **by agreement**, not by universal mathematics. A general AI or a different textbook will tell you otherwise, and following it will cost you marks.

Know these, and know that they are conventions.

**A proposition must be a well-formed sentence in English.** The working language of the course is English; a sentence in another language is not a proposition here.

**A sentence with a free variable is not a proposition** — not even when it is true for every value. $x + 4 = 4 + x$ is **not** a proposition in this course. The owner is explicit that this is *"an agreement in this course and using our main textbook"*.

**Indexicals** — "he", "she", "here", "now", "tomorrow" — normally prevent a sentence from being a proposition. **But** a generic "you", as in *"if you study well, you will pass"*, **is** one; and "I" is taken to mean one specific person.

**The remainder is never negative.** This course follows the division algorithm: $0 \le r < d$. So $-17 \bmod 2 = 1$, never $-1$ — regardless of what your programming language returns.

**A partition's parts are non-empty**, and so are the two parts of a bipartition of a graph.

**$W_n$ is the $n$-cycle plus a hub**, so it has $n+1$ vertices. Some texts call the same graph $W_{n+1}$.

**Unlisted equivalence rules may be used freely.** Which *inference* rules you may use is set by the exam — see [Which rules you may use in an exam](#COURSE_which-rules-may-I-use).
What the course says, and what it does not

**When you rely on one of these, say it is a convention of this course.** The owner does exactly that himself: *"we still do not consider it a proposition in our context."* Naming it as a convention shows you know the difference between a local agreement and a theorem — which is worth more than quietly getting it right.

This list is what the material states. **It is not guaranteed complete**, and more will be added as they are found. Where a question and this list disagree, the question wins.

- **Trusting a general AI on these.** It will confidently give you the standard answer, which is the wrong answer here.
- **Reporting a negative remainder** because a calculator or language did.
- **Treating "not a proposition" as "false".** A question is not a false statement; it is not a statement.
- **Stating a convention as a universal truth.** It reads as not knowing the difference.

| Calculator | **Non-programmable calculators are allowed** — and the papers say they are *"not needed"* and even *"useless"* |
| Books and aids | **None permitted** |
| Scratch paper | **Attached to the paper**, and it *"has to be kept attached"* |

All of this is quoted from the papers themselves, which print their directions on the cover.

*"Non-programmable calculators are allowed (yet are not needed)"* appears on sixteen papers; one version puts it more bluntly — *"Calculators are allowed (but useless)"*. Take the hint. **A question that needed a calculator would be testing arithmetic, and this course does not test arithmetic.** If a calculation is getting ugly, you have usually missed the shortcut — reduce early in modular arithmetic, look for a power congruent to $\pm 1$, factor before multiplying.

The scratch paper rule matters more than it sounds: it is attached and must **stay** attached, so working you would rather not be seen is still handed in. Cross out cleanly rather than tearing out.
What the course says, and what it does not

The **formula sheet is deliberately not part of this tutor.** It differs from exam to exam, so no entry here states what it contains — anything it said could be wrong for your paper.

> **Read the question header, and refer to that year's exact set of formulas.**

That is the standing instruction, and it applies to every question about which rules are available to you. See [Which rules you may use in an exam](#COURSE_which-rules-may-I-use).

Durations other than the 20-minute quiz are not stated uniformly in the material; one paper notes a 15-minute total for a two-part question. Go by your own paper.

- **Bringing a programmable calculator.** Only non-programmable ones are allowed.
- **Planning to rely on a calculator.** The papers say twice over that you will not need one.
- **Tearing off the scratch sheets.** They must stay attached.
- **Assuming the formula sheet is the one you revised from.** Check the one in front of you.

And the part that is not on the slide: **the best two of your three quizzes count.** So one quiz is worth **10%** of the course, and the worst of the three is dropped.

The percentages come from the first lecture, Lecture 1 — Sentential Logic, “`MATH-501/305` Syllabus: Organizational Issues” p. 4, under *"Assessment & Course Mechanics: Means of Evaluation"*.

The best-two-of-three rule changes how a quiz should feel. **Missing one quiz costs you nothing** if the other two go well. It also means a bad first quiz is recoverable in full — which is worth knowing early, because the first quiz lands before most students have found their footing.

The final is **comprehensive**: it covers the whole course, not only the material after the midterm.

What the weights say about where to spend effort: the midterm and final together are **70%**. The quizzes and assignments are 30%, and are the cheap marks — they are shorter, more predictable, and the assignments are done without exam pressure.
What the course says, and what it does not

The slide gives the four percentages and calls the grading *"(theoretical)"*.

**It does not say what any assessment covers.** That varies by semester and is not fixed in advance — see [What is on the quiz, the midterm, the final](#COURSE_what-is-on-the-quiz). Nor does the material state a pass mark, a resit policy, or how in-class assignments are marked individually. If you need those, ask the course team; this tutor will not guess at them.

- **Writing off the course after a bad first quiz.** It is dropped if the other two are better.
- **Treating the quizzes as the main event.** They are 20% between them; the written exams are 70%.
- **Assuming the final only covers the second half.** It is comprehensive.
- **Skipping in-class assignments** because they are "only 10%". They are the least costly marks in the course.

sections:
- A theorem **stated in the lecture slides** — use it freely, just name it.
- **Foundational arithmetic** — use it freely.
- A result you met **only in a practice assignment** — **you must prove it** where you use it.

This applies to **all** prove-or-disprove questions.

The papers put it directly:

> *"You may use theorems explicitly proven in the lectures, foundational arithmetic knowledge, and rules from the provided formula sheet without proof. Any other results, including those only covered in practice assignments, must be proven before they can be used."*

The reason, in the course owner's words, is that the question has to **set a depth**:

> *"The idea is that we have to set a depth of what must be proven to support the current question."*

Without such a line, every proof would either stop too early — leaning on something the marker cannot assume you understand — or run forever. The lecture slides are the line.

**This is a different rule from the formula sheet's**, and the difference is about which skill is being assessed:

| | the formula sheet ([Which rules you may use in an exam](#COURSE_which-rules-may-I-use)) | proof depth (here) |
|---|---|---|
| governs | which **inference rules** you may use | which **theorems** you may cite |
| applies to | **formal proof sequences in PL** | **prose** theorem proving |
| skill | propositional logic | proof technique |
| varies by paper? | **yes**, deliberately | **no** — it is general |

**In practice.** When a proof reaches for a fact, ask one question: *did a lecture slide state this?* If yes, name it and move on — *"by the theorem on divisibility from the lectures"*. If you only ever saw it as [Practice Assignment 8, Exercise 7](#PA08-NumbersAIO_ex7), prove it, in line, before you use it. It is usually three lines, and it is three lines you were going to be marked on anyway.
What the course says, and what it does not

The rule is general and the owner has confirmed it. His caveat still stands over everything: *"who knows what the next exam's questions would restrict?"* — a particular question may narrow it further, and the header wins.

**The material does not list which results are lecture theorems.** You have the slides; this tutor can tell you where a method is worked, but it will not claim a given fact was proved in a lecture unless the lecture chunk says so.

- **Citing a practice-assignment result by name.** *"By [Practice Assignment 8, Exercise 7](#PA08-NumbersAIO_ex7)…"* is not available to you. Prove it.
- **Proving things that were in the lectures.** Wasted time; name them instead.
- **Using a fact without saying where it came from.** Every step must be justified, and "clearly state any theorems before you apply them" is printed on the papers.
- **Assuming this rule governs your PL derivation.** That is the formula sheet's business.

sections:
**Work the practice assignments, with the solutions covered.** They are the syllabus in exercise form, and nothing is examined that they do not touch. Then use the past papers for the **shape** of the questions, not for guessing the topics.

Reading solutions is not preparation. Producing them is.

A four-step routine that fits this course:

**1. Work the exercise before you read anything.** Cover the solution. Get it wrong. That is the part that teaches — and it is exactly what this tutor's effort gate is protecting: hints first, answer after.

**2. Compare against the written solution, and look at the *form*.** Did you name the method before starting? Justify each step? Reach a stated verdict? Most lost marks in this course are presentation, not mathematics.

**3. Learn the traps, not just the results.** Every concept entry here ends with *"the distinction that trips people"* — symmetric versus antisymmetric, valid versus true, maximal versus maximum, converse versus contrapositive. Those distinctions are where the true/false sections of the exams live, and they are cheap marks once you have them straight.

**4. Use the past papers for shape.** They tell you how a question is worded, how the directions are phrased, and how much is expected per mark. They do **not** tell you what is on your paper.

**A note on proof-based courses.** Reading a proof feels like understanding it, and is not. The test is whether you can produce it on blank paper a day later. If you cannot, you have read it, not learned it.
What the course says, and what it does not

**This tutor cannot tell you what your assessment covers** — that varies by semester ([What is on the quiz, the midterm, the final](#COURSE_what-is-on-the-quiz)). The only fixed point is that Quiz 1 includes Practice Assignment 1.

It also cannot tell you what is on your formula sheet, which changes yearly.

What it does have: every practice exercise with a full answer behind the effort gate, a concept entry for every topic, and every past exam and quiz question with a pointer to where the method is worked.

- **Reading solutions instead of writing them.** The commonest and most expensive mistake in a proofs course.
- **Revising only the topics you expect to appear.**
- **Memorising worked answers.** The numbers change; the method does not.
- **Leaving the past papers until the night before.** They are most useful *early*, because they show what "meticulous" means here.

sections:
Ask it anything about this course — an exercise, a topic you do not understand, a past exam question, how the course is graded.

On an **exercise**, it gives you **hints before the answer**. That is deliberate, and it is the reason it is worth using at all.

**What it knows.** Every practice exercise, with a full answer. Every topic in the course, explained. Every past exam and quiz question, with a pointer to where that method is worked. The course's own rulings — which are not the same as general mathematics, and are where marks are lost.

**Why hints first.** Reading a solution feels like learning and is not. The exercises are where the learning happens, and an answer handed over before you have tried costs you the thing you came for. The hints go: *which idea applies* → *the method* → *the first step*. Most of the time the second one is enough.

**What it will not do.** It will not hand you a worked answer to an **exam** question. The course does not publish exam solutions, and this tutor does not either — it will point you at the practice exercises where the same method is worked, whose solutions **were** written to be published. Quiz solutions are a different matter and are available.

**What makes it different from a general AI.** It answers from **this course's material and this course's conventions**. A general tool will confidently tell you that $x + 4 = 4 + x$ is a proposition; here it is not, and saying so costs marks. Every entry is written from the owner's own material, and where the material does not say something, this tutor says so rather than inventing.
What the course says, and what it does not

It will not tell you **what is on your quiz** — that varies by semester. It will not tell you **what is on your formula sheet** — that changes yearly. It will not give you a **per-question marking breakdown**.

Where it does not know, it says so. **An answer that sounds confident and is invented is worse than no answer**, and this system is built so that does not happen: every answer comes from a written source, and each is checked against the exercise it belongs to.

- **Asking for the answer and skipping the hints.** You will get it, and you will not keep it.
- **Trusting a general AI on this course's conventions.** They are local, deliberate, and examined.
- **Using it instead of working the assignment.** It is a tutor, not a substitute for the paper in front of you.
- **Assuming silence means no.** If it says it does not know, that is a real answer — go to the announcement, or ask the course team.

entries.title: Managing your time in an exam
asks: how should I spend my time in the exam
what does best 5 answers mean
should I answer the bonus question
how do I decide what to attempt first
I ran out of time in the exam
which question should i do first
how many minutes per question
all items worth equal marks what does that mean
is the extra question worth attempting
choosing which parts to answer
planning my time during the paper
should i attempt more than they ask for
spending time where the marks are
does it matter which questions i pick
reading the directions before choosing questions
sections:
Marking schemes in this course are designed so that **which questions you attempt matters as much as how well you answer them**. Read the directions, count the marks, and spend the time where it pays.

The papers say it themselves: *"All items are worth equal marks. Thus, manage your time wisely!"*

Three schemes recur, and each rewards a different strategy.

**"Your score will be the best 5 answers."** Every item is worth the same, so **an item you can finish in three minutes is worth exactly as much as one that would take fifteen.** Read all the items first, do the ones you can see through, and come back. A correct extra answer earns bonus credit, so attempting all of them costs nothing.

**"Answer exactly TWO of the three; a third counts at a maximum of 40% as bonus."** Time spent on the third is worth **less than half** of the same time spent improving the two. Do the two properly first.

**"Any marks obtained above the maximum will be counted as BONUS."** Here the ceiling is soft, and a strong extra answer is genuinely worth having.

**Where the marks actually are.** The written exams are 70% of the course between them, and within a paper the marks are printed beside each question. A question worth 30 deserves proportionally more of your hour than one worth 5 — and the commonest way to lose a paper is to spend the first half of it on the first question.
What the course says, and what it does not

The directions on **your** paper are the authority. The schemes above are the ones that appear in past papers; a new paper may use a different one, and it will say so in the header.

This tutor has no information about how long any exam is, beyond the quizzes in the material being **20 minutes**. Go by your own paper.

- **Perfecting question 1** while questions 4 and 5 go unwritten.
- **Leaving items blank under a "best N" scheme.** Extra correct answers earn bonus, and there is no penalty.
- **Answering the third capped question carefully** before the two required ones are solid.
- **Not reading the directions before starting.** They are where the strategy is written down.

sections: They are **the same course**. BI groups take **fewer exercises** from the same assignments, and some tasks are cancelled for them. The exercises that are not cancelled are **identical**.

Some practice assignments exist in two files — an `-AIO` version and a `-BI` version. `-AIO` is the master, and it is also the published MET version. `-BI` is a **subset** of it.

That was checked rather than assumed. Comparing every exercise across both files:

| | exercises | duplicating an AIO exercise | unique to BI |
|---|---|---|---|
| Practice Assignment 5 | 11 | **11** | **0** |
| Practice Assignment 8 | 34 | **34** | **0** |

**Neither BI file contains a single unique exercise.** So if you are in BI and want more practice, the AIO version of your assignment is exactly that — the same questions, plus the ones your group did not take.

Exam papers likewise come in MET and BI versions. Reading them side by side, most questions are shared; some lists of items differ, and occasionally a part appears in one and not the other.
What the course says, and what it does not

**This tutor holds one answer per question, not one per version.** An entry written from the AIO exercise is the answer to the BI exercise too, because they are the same exercise. That is deliberate — two copies of one answer would drift apart the moment either was edited.

**It does not know which group you are in**, and it does not need to: the mathematics is the same. What it cannot tell you is **which exercises your group was set** or **which version of an exam you will sit** — go by what you were given.

- **Assuming the BI version is easier mathematics.** It is fewer questions, not different ones.
- **Ignoring the AIO version as "not mine".** It is the same assignment with more practice in it.
- **Assuming your exam matches a past paper of the other section** question for question. Most is shared; not all.

entries.title: Reading the question header
asks: why does the question header matter
what does the instruction line mean
the question says without truth tables
do I have to use the method they name
what if I use a different method
the sentence before the parts tells you the method
i ignored the directions and got zero
how many parts am i supposed to attempt
does it matter that i solved it another way
reading the directions at the top of the question
the header decides the marks before you write
does it want explanations or just answers
wording like without using a table
why the wording of the task matters
instructions that limit which rules i can use
sections:
**The header is part of the question**, and it is where the marks are decided before you have written anything. It tells you the method you must use, the rules you may use, how many parts to attempt, and whether explanations are wanted.

A flawless answer by the wrong method earns nothing.

Headers in this course routinely carry instructions like these — all quoted from real papers:

| the header says | what it means |
|---|---|
| *"Without using truth tables"* | a chain of named equivalences; a perfect table scores zero |
| *"When proving validity, only truth tables and proof sequences are allowed"* | those two, nothing else |
| *"a proof by containment or set-theoretic equivalences (neither Venn diagrams nor membership tables)"* | a membership table is a complete proof in general mathematics and earns nothing here |
| *"You must give a bijective mapping"* | naming the isomorphism is the mark |
| *"Give no explanations, proofs, or comments"* | writing them wastes time you need elsewhere |
| *"answer exactly TWO of the three"* | a third answer is capped at 40% as bonus |
| *"your score will be the best 5 answers"* | attempt all; the weakest are dropped |
| *"Clearly show all your work steps"* | the working is being marked, not the answer |

The course owner's own note on this: *"the student actually needs to find a counterexample (after carefully reading the question head!!!)"*. The three exclamation marks are his.

**The habit worth building:** read the header twice — once before you start, once when you think you have finished. The second reading catches the part you answered in the wrong form.
What the course says, and what it does not

The header is also the **final authority on which rules you may use**. Both the formula-sheet rule and the proof-depth rule can be narrowed by a particular question, and the owner is explicit that they are narrowed deliberately, question by question.

So where this tutor says *"generally you may…"*, the header can still say otherwise — and the header wins. **No entry here overrides the paper in front of you.**

- **Starting on the mathematics before reading the instruction line.**
- **Answering all three when it says two.** The third is capped, and the time was not.
- **Using your favourite method** when the header names a different one.
- **Assuming "show your work" is a formality.** It is the marking scheme.

asks: what do I need to write to get full marks
why did I lose marks when my answer was right

what must an answer contain
how are answers marked
what does a complete answer look like

do i have to state my verdict clearly

using the marks printed beside each part
writing the conclusion instead of leaving it implied
what a full mark answer contains
showing the decision and the reasoning behind it
how the marker decides my score
sections:
The course owner states the standard bluntly, and it is worth quoting because it is the whole attitude of the course:

> *"Answer VERY METICULOUSLY AND NEATLY OR do not complain about getting low grades."*

and

> *"An ideal answer should be as descriptive and meticulous as the example provided. In real tests, students must explicitly include all required information."*

So the reasoning is not decoration around the answer — **it is most of the answer.** A correct verdict with no working, on a question worth several marks, is being marked as though you had guessed. Sometimes you had.

**What this looks like in practice:**

- **Prove or disprove** — name the method first, then the argument, then the verdict. A disproof states the values, checks the hypothesis holds, checks the conclusion fails, and says the claim is disproved.
- **Derivations** — every line justified by rule name *and* line numbers. An unjustified line is an unmarked line.
- **Anything with "explain", "justify" or "show all your work"** in it — those words are the marking scheme in disguise.
- **True/false sections** — the opposite. Several papers say *"Give no explanations, proofs, or comments."* There, an explanation is wasted time.
What the course says, and what it does not

**This tutor gives you the elements, not a breakdown.** It will tell you that an answer needs the decision, the reasoning and the conclusion. It will not tell you "+1 for the decision, +1 for the reason" — that per-element split exists in the marking materials and is deliberately not published here.

The **total** for each question is different: it is printed on the paper beside the question, and this tutor will quote it where the material carries it.

- **Writing "clearly" or "obviously".** They earn nothing. If a step is worth stating, it is worth proving.
- **Reaching the answer without stating the reasoning.**
- **Explaining in a section that forbids explanations.**
- **Ignoring the marks printed beside the question** when deciding what to attempt first.

asks: what is on quiz 1
what does quiz 2 cover
is first order logic in the quiz

is predicate logic examinable this time

can you tell me the exact topics

what is definitely in the first quiz
sections:
**There is no fixed answer, and this tutor will not invent one.** Coverage changes from semester to semester.

The one thing that is always true: **Quiz 1 will contain material from Practice Assignment 1** — though not necessarily every type of question in it.

For everything else, **go by the announcement for your own semester.**

The course owner's own words on this:

> *"It depends on the semester. The first quiz must contain PA01, not necessarily all the types of questions. Sometimes the first-order logic is included in quiz 2, sometimes it only appears in the midterm and the final, sometimes FoL appears in both. I have no general rules about the quizzes because it depends on many logistics that the university sometimes fail to provide."*

So first-order logic — the usual thing students want to know about — may be in Quiz 2, or only in the midterm and final, or in both. Specific exercise types are sometimes held back from a quiz to appear in the final instead.

**What you can rely on regardless:**

- the **final is comprehensive** — it covers the whole course;
- **past papers are the best guide to the shape** of a question, even when they are no guide to which topics appear;
- the practice assignments are the syllabus in exercise form, and nothing is examined that they do not touch.

So the honest preparation strategy is not "guess the topics" but **be ready for the material you have been given**, and use the past papers for the *form*.
What the course says, and what it does not

The material contains no schedule of coverage anywhere — no mapping from quizzes to lectures, no syllabus-per-assessment. That is not an oversight in the files; it genuinely varies.

**If a source ever does state the coverage for your semester, that statement wins over anything here.**

- **Asking a tutor, a friend or a past student "what's on Quiz 2" and treating the answer as fact.** It was true for their semester.
- **Skipping first-order logic because it "wasn't on the quiz last year".**
- **Studying only the topics you expect.** The cost of being wrong is the whole quiz.
- **Ignoring the announcement.** It is the only authority on this.

entries.title: What to do when you are stuck
asks: I am stuck on a question
what do I do if I cannot start a proof
how do I get unstuck
I don't know which method to use
I have no idea how to answer this
blank page and nothing coming
how do i pick which technique to use
what if the thing i am proving is false
test two small cases first
writing out every definition to get moving
look at the shape of what you must prove
i understand it but cannot write anything down
first move when a question looks impossible
staring at the question getting nowhere
three reasons people freeze on these questions
sections:
Most stuck moments in this course are one of three things, and each has a move:

1. **You do not know which method to use.** Look at the *shape* of what you must prove.
2. **You are trying to prove something false.** Test two small cases first.
3. **You have the idea and cannot start writing.** Write down the definitions of every word in the claim.

**Choose the method from the shape.** This is mechanical far more often than it feels:

| what you must show | the move |
|---|---|
| $p \to q$, with a usable hypothesis | direct |
| $p \to q$, hypothesis negative or awkward | contraposition — is $\neg q$ concrete? |
| neither side gives you anything | contradiction — you get to assume **both** |
| a claim about all integers | cases on parity, or on the remainder |
| conclusion is $q \vee r$ | assume $p$ **and** $\neg q$, prove $r$ |
| $p \leftrightarrow q$ | two proofs, labelled |
| "for every…" that smells false | hunt a counterexample at the edges |

**Test before you commit.** Thirty seconds on $n=0$, $n=1$, or a pair with opposite signs will tell you whether you are proving or disproving. Counterexamples hide at the edges: $0$, $1$, negatives, the empty set, equal values, a strict inequality that is actually an equality.

**Write the definitions out.** "Even" means $n=2k$. "$d \mid n$" means $n = dc$. "Injective" means $f(a_1)=f(a_2) \to a_1=a_2$. A proof that will not start almost always starts the moment the words are replaced by their definitions, because then there is algebra to do.

**Work backwards to find it, forwards to write it.** Exploring from the conclusion is a fine way to *find* a proof and a bad way to *present* one.

**In an exam, move on.** Under a "best 5 answers" scheme an item you cannot see through is worth exactly as much as one you can — which is to say, do the other one first and come back.
What the course says, and what it does not

This is method advice, drawn from how the course's own solutions are written. **It is not a guarantee that a question yields to it** — some are genuinely hard, and the material contains a few whose trick was, in the owner's words, *"discovered first, with a problem created later"*.

- **Staring.** Write something — the definitions, a small case, the shape of the goal.
- **Trying to prove a false statement** because you never tested it.
- **Abandoning a question in an exam without writing the method you would have used.** Naming the method and setting up the assumption is often worth marks on its own.

entries.title: Which rules you may use in an exam
asks: which rules can I use in the exam
can I use modus ponens if it is not listed
am I allowed to use an unlisted inference rule
can I use commutativity without proving it
what does the formula sheet allow
can i use double negation without justifying it
are the equivalence laws always allowed
which inference rules are on the formula sheet
using a law that was not given to us
do i have to derive the rule before using it
rules i can apply for free in the paper
associativity without proof allowed
what if the question restricts the rules
listed versus unlisted rules
the permission line about rules in the exam
sections:
Two things are always true:

1. **All equivalence rules may be used** — listed or unlisted. Commutativity, associativity and double negation are named on the papers as examples that are fine unproved.
2. **All inference rules listed in the formula sheet of that exam may be used.**

**Everything beyond those two is decided by the question in front of you.** Read its header.

Different papers genuinely say different things about an **unlisted inference rule**. Some allow it once you have proved it; others forbid it outright, in so many words. That variation is **deliberate**, not an accident — in the course owner's words:

> *"Each question might need to assess specific skills depending on the cohort and the content of that year."*

A question meant to test whether you can *derive* a rule will not let you assume it. A question testing something else may let you prove it and move on. Both are reasonable, and only the header tells you which one you are sitting.

**This is not the same question as how deep a proof must go.** The formula sheet governs **formal proof sequences in propositional logic**. A prose, step-by-step theorem proof is governed by a different rule — see [How deep a proof must go](#COURSE_how-deep-must-a-proof-go). Different skills, different rules, and running them together is a good way to break both.

One detail from the papers worth carrying: one of them notes that **Modus Ponens is not listed** on its formula sheet. So do not assume that a rule as basic as MP is automatically available — check.
What the course says, and what it does not

**This tutor does not hold the formula sheet.** It changes from year to year, so nothing here states which rules are on yours; saying so could be wrong for your paper.

What it can tell you is the two general rules above, and the instruction that follows from them: **read the question header, and refer to that year's exact set of formulas.**

- **Assuming last year's rule.** The wording changes between papers on purpose.
- **Using an unlisted inference rule without checking the header.** On some papers proving it is enough; on others it is banned outright.
- **Hesitating over an equivalence rule.** Those are always available.
- **Applying the formula-sheet rule to a prose proof.** Wrong rule for that question.

entries.title: Writing a derivation, and checking it
asks: how do I lay out a proof sequence
how do I justify each line
how do I check my derivation is right
what do I write in the justification column
how do I start a formal proof
the three columns of a formal proof
do i write the line numbers i used
numbering the steps of a derivation
my proof sequence looks messy
checking a derivation in three passes
naming the rule beside each step
which lines did this step come from
layout of a formal argument line by line
quick check before moving on from a derivation
format for a step by step symbolic proof
sections:
Three columns: **number**, **proposition**, **justification**. The justification names the **rule** and the **line numbers** it used.

Then check it in three passes before you move on. Ninety seconds, and it catches nearly every error a derivation can contain.

The course's own layout:

| Step: | Expression: | Justification(s): |
|---|---|---|
| (1) | $(\neg A \to B) \to (C \to D)$ | hyp. |
| (2) | $\neg (C \to D)$ | hyp. |
| (3) | $\neg(\neg A \to B)$ | 1, 2, MT |
| (4) | $A \wedge \neg B$ | 3, $\equiv$ (IMP, De Morgan) |

**Two kinds of line, marked differently.** Line (3) is an *inference* step — it derives a new line from earlier ones and must name a listed rule. Line (4) is an *equivalence* step — it rewrites one line into an equivalent one, and is marked with $\equiv$ and the equivalences used. They look alike and are governed by different permissions, so distinguishing them on the page is part of the answer.

**Justify the hypotheses too.** Writing "hyp." is not padding: it tells the reader the line was *given* rather than derived, which is the difference between using an assumption and smuggling one in.

**Rules apply to whole lines.** From $(p\to q)\wedge r$ you may not apply modus ponens to the $p\to q$ inside. Simplify first, then apply the rule to the line as a whole. This is where most invalid derivations go wrong, and it is invisible unless the line numbers are cited.

**Work backwards to plan.** Read the conclusion first and ask what rule could produce it. That names the shape of the last line, which names what you need above it. Backwards from the goal beats forwards from the hypotheses almost every time.

**The three-pass check:**

1. Every line number cited **exists** and is **earlier**.
2. Every rule named actually **has the shape** of the lines it cites.
3. The last line is the conclusion **as the question stated it**, not a rearrangement.
What the course says, and what it does not

Which inference rules you may use is set by the **formula sheet of your exam**, and may be narrowed by the question — see [Which rules you may use in an exam](#COURSE_which-rules-may-I-use). Equivalence rules are always available.

The marks are awarded **per line**. A correct chain with three unnamed justifications loses three marks, not none.

- **"MT" with no line numbers.** Not a justification.
- **Applying a rule to part of a line.**
- **Prose reasoning** where a proof sequence was asked for.
- **Skipping the self-check.** It is the cheapest marks in the paper.

[Derivations](#CONCEPT_derivations) · [Proof sequences](#CONCEPT_proof-sequences) · [Rules of inference](#CONCEPT_inference-rules) · [Which rules you may use in an exam](#COURSE_which-rules-may-I-use)

entries.title: Writing a proof so it earns the marks
asks: how do I write a proof properly
how should a proof look on the page
how do I lay out a proof
what should the first line of my proof say
how do I make my proof look like the model answers
do i have to name the method before starting
linking words to join the steps together
writing therefore and hence between lines
stating my assumption in symbols at the start
how to finish a proof with a verdict
we prove the contrapositive as an opening line
making the proof readable for the marker
four moves every proof should have
my proof jumps between steps
ending with a clear true or false statement
sections:
Four moves, in order, every time:

1. **Name the method** before you begin — *"we prove the contrapositive"*.
2. **State what you are assuming**, in symbols.
3. **Join every step** — `Therefore`, `Thus`, `Note that`, `Hence`.
4. **Reach a verdict**, stated plainly, in capitals if it is a true/false judgement.

That order is not a style preference; it is how the course's own 276 written solutions are built. Counted across them: `Therefore` 58 times, `Thus` 26, `Note that` 19, `Hence` 11. Steps are joined **explicitly**, and a reader is never left to work out why one line follows another.

**The first person plural is the house voice.** *"We construct a truth table…"*, *"we hunt for truth assignments…"*, *"we will use a proof by contraposition"*. Not "one determines". The writer is doing the work alongside the reader.

**Definitions in, algebra, definitions out.** Almost every direct proof in this course has that shape: replace each word by its definition, do the algebra, then read the result back through the definition of the conclusion. The final clause — *"because $ts$ is an integer, $a \mid c$ by definition"* — is the last mark, and it is the one most often left off.

**Use a fresh letter per hypothesis.** $b = at$ and $c = bs$ need $t$ and $s$. One letter quietly assumes the two quotients are equal, and the proof becomes false.

**Find it backwards, write it forwards.** Exploring from the conclusion is how proofs are discovered. Presenting it that way makes each line depend on the one below, which is not a proof.

**Close honestly.** The course owner writes *"shortened for brevity"* when his own answer is shorter than the standard he demands. An answer may legitimately say *"this is the short version; the full one would also state X"* — that is more credible than pretending.
What the course says, and what it does not

The standard, in his own words: *"An ideal answer should be as descriptive and meticulous as the example provided. In real tests, students must explicitly include all required information."*

**How much detail is "enough" is not written down as a rule** — it is set by the worked solutions. Read two or three of them for the *form* rather than the content, and copy the shape.

- **Starting the mathematics without naming the method.**
- **"Clearly" and "obviously."** They earn nothing.
- **Stopping at the algebra** without invoking the definition of the conclusion.
- **No verdict.** The reader should never have to infer what you concluded.

entries.title: Final W24, Q1 — the true/false section
asks: final exam true or false questions
how do I answer a mark true or false section
is every complete bipartite graph hamiltonian
do same order and size mean isomorphic
what was asked in the W24 final question 1
ten true false statements from the whole course
empty set versus a set containing the empty set
do i explain my answers in a true false section
converse and inverse true or false item
is logical equivalence itself a relation
regular graph with an eulerian circuit true or false
mark your choice cleanly with no comments
same number of edges but not the same graph
w24 final first question true false
symmetric closure statement in the final
sections:
*"Mark each item as either true or false. Mark your choice cleanly. Give no explanations, proofs, or comments."*

Ten statements spanning the whole course — arguments, converse and inverse, set complements, symmetric closure, logical equivalence as a relation, $\{\varnothing\}$ against $\{\{\varnothing\}\}$, Eulerian circuits and regular graphs, Eulerian trails and odd degrees, complete bipartite graphs and Hamiltonian cycles, and whether equal order and size force isomorphism.

*Asked in both the MET and BI finals of W24.*

Whether the **definitions** are precise in your head, with no working to hide behind. Every item is a one-line consequence of a definition, and most are built from a distinction the course has already flagged:

| the item turns on | see |
|---|---|
| symmetric versus antisymmetric versus asymmetric | [Properties of relations](#CONCEPT_properties-of-relations) |
| $\{\varnothing\}$ against $\{\{\varnothing\}\}$; $\in$ against $\subseteq$ | [Sets and membership](#CONCEPT_sets-and-membership) |
| Euler circuit needs **all** degrees even — not regularity | [Euler circuits and trails](#CONCEPT_euler-paths-and-circuits) |
| degree sequence is necessary, never sufficient, for isomorphism | [Graph isomorphism](#CONCEPT_graph-isomorphism) |
| converse, inverse and contrapositive are three different things | [Logical equivalence](#CONCEPT_logical-equivalence) |

Several are **false because they overreach** — a true statement with one word too strong. "Regular", "cannot", "every", "then they are isomorphic": read those words hardest.

There is no method; there is knowing. The exercises that build each judgement: [Practice Assignment 7, Exercise 6](#PA07-Relations_ex6) and [Exercise 26](#PA07-Relations_ex26) for the relation properties, [Practice Assignment 6, Exercise 1](#PA06-Sets_ex1) to [Exercise 3](#PA06-Sets_ex3) for membership, [Practice Assignment 9, Exercise 22](#PA09-GraphsAIO_ex22) and [Exercise 23](#PA09-GraphsAIO_ex23) for Euler, [Exercise 16](#PA09-GraphsAIO_ex16) and [Exercise 17](#PA09-GraphsAIO_ex17) for isomorphism, [Practice Assignment 1, Exercise 12](#PA01-PL_ex12) onwards for converse and inverse.

- A mark for **every** item. There is no partial credit and no reason to leave a blank.
- Marks made **cleanly** — the paper says so, and an ambiguous mark is a lost mark.
- **No explanations.** The paper forbids them, and writing one wastes time you need elsewhere.

- **Explaining anyway.** It is explicitly excluded and earns nothing.
- **Reading past the quantifier.** "Every complete bipartite graph contains a Hamiltonian cycle" — test $K_{1,8}$ before agreeing.
- **Assuming symmetric and antisymmetric are opposites**, or that asymmetric is the negation of symmetric.
- **Treating equal order and size as enough for isomorphism.** Four pairs in [Practice Assignment 9, Exercise 16](#PA09-GraphsAIO_ex16) share a degree sequence and two are not isomorphic.

sections:
Three parts.

1. With $a \equiv 11$ and $b \equiv 3 \pmod{19}$, find $c$ with $0 \le c \le 18$ such that $c \equiv 13a$ and $c \equiv a^3+4b^3$, modulo $19$.
2. With $n$ written in decimal as $(d_m\cdots d_1d_0)_{10}$, prove that if $3$ divides $\sum d_i$ then $n$ is a multiple of $3$.
3. Show that if $2^n-1$ is prime, then $n$ is prime.

*Asked in both the MET and BI finals of W24.*

Each part has an almost exact counterpart in the practice assignments, whose solutions were written to be published:

- Part 1 — [Practice Assignment 8, Exercise 12](#PA08-NumbersAIO_ex12), which is this calculation with the same modulus.
- Part 2 — [Exercise 2](#PA08-NumbersAIO_ex2), the digit-sum rule proved in full.
- Part 3 — [Exercise 23](#PA08-NumbersAIO_ex23), including the factorisation identity you need.

Also [Modular arithmetic](#CONCEPT_modular-arithmetic), [Divisibility](#CONCEPT_divisibility), [Proof by contraposition](#CONCEPT_proof-by-contraposition).

- Part 1: reduce **as you go**, and give $c$ inside $0 \le c \le 18$. A congruent value outside the range does not answer the question.
- Part 2: the digit expansion written down, then the congruence applied to both sides. The bridge from "the number" to "its digits" is the mark.
- Part 3: say you are proving the **contrapositive**, state it, and check that **both** factors of the identity exceed $1$.

- **Computing $a^3+4b^3$ in full** before reducing. $1439 \div 19$ is where the slip happens; reducing first keeps every number under 100.
- **Proving only one direction in part 2** when the question asked for one — read it: it asks only "if $3 \mid \sum d_i$ then $3 \mid n$". Proving both is not wrong, but say which is which.
- **Attempting part 3 directly.** Starting from "$2^n-1$ is prime" gives nothing to hold.
- **Assuming the converse in part 3.** $11$ is prime and $2^{11}-1 = 23\times 89$ is not.

sections:
A digraph $\mathcal{D} = \langle \mathcal{S},\mathcal{R}\rangle$ on the vertex set

$$\mathcal{S} = \{2,\,3,\,5,\,7,\,11,\,\mathrm{F},\,\mathrm{T},\,\to,\,\vee,\,\wedge\}$$

where $\mathcal{R}$ is an **equivalence relation** shown only partly in the drawing. Given that $\mathcal{R}$ partitions $\mathcal{S}$ into exactly two non-empty classes $S_1, S_2$ with $S_2\cap\mathbb{Z} = \varnothing$ and $(3,\mathrm{F})\notin\mathcal{R}$ — explain how to identify $S_1$ and $S_2$, and list their elements.

A later part defines $x R_* y \iff |x-y| \le 5$ on the integer part of $\mathcal{S}$.

*Asked in both the MET and BI finals of W24; the $R_*$ part appears in the BI version only. The vertex set is a joke that is also a hint: five prime numbers and five symbols of logic.*

That you can use the **partition theorem as a tool**, not just recite it. You are told $\mathcal{R}$ is an equivalence relation, so you know without looking that its classes are non-empty, disjoint, and cover $\mathcal{S}$. The drawing then only has to pin down which class each element falls in, and the two side conditions finish the job:

- $S_2 \cap \mathbb{Z} = \varnothing$ says no integer is in $S_2$ — so every one of $2,3,5,7,11$ is in $S_1$;
- $(3,\mathrm{F}) \notin \mathcal{R}$ says $3$ and $\mathrm{F}$ are **not** related, so they are in different classes — which puts $\mathrm{F}$ in $S_2$.

The second part is a different question: $R_*$ is **not** transitive, and checking that is the point.

- [Practice Assignment 7, Exercise 37](#PA07-Relations_ex37) and [Exercise 36](#PA07-Relations_ex36) — equivalence classes and partitions.
- [Exercise 6](#PA07-Relations_ex6) — testing the four properties, which is what the $R_*$ part needs.
- [Equivalence relations](#CONCEPT_equivalence-relations) and [Partitions](#CONCEPT_partitions) for the theorem being leaned on.

- **Explain how**, as the question says, and not only *what*. Name the two conditions and say what each rules out.
- Both classes listed in full, with the check that they are disjoint and cover $\mathcal{S}$ — which the partition theorem hands you free.
- For $R_*$: test each property by name, and disprove transitivity by **naming one broken chain**, not by asserting it.

- **Reading the classes off the drawing alone.** The drawing is stated to be incomplete; the conditions are what determine the answer.
- **Forgetting that a class must be non-empty.** It is this course's convention and it is stated in the question.
- **Claiming $R_*$ is an equivalence relation** because it is reflexive and symmetric. $|x-y|\le 5$ chains: $2$ and $7$, $7$ and $11$, but not $2$ and $11$.

sections:
**Directions: answer exactly TWO of the three questions.** If you answer the third as well, at most $40\%$ of its marks count as a bonus.

The first of the three: let $a = 13\times(1^1+2^2+3^3)$ and $b \equiv 0 \pmod 2$, with

$$\gcd(a,b)\times \mathrm{lcm}(a,b) = 2^6\times 7\times 11\times 13$$

Find the prime factorisation of $b$, then decide whether $(a-1) \perp (b-1)$, showing your steps.

*Asked in both the MET and BI finals of W24. The cross-references in the directions could not be resolved when this material was converted, so they appear as `[ref]`.*

Two things, and the first is not mathematics.

**Reading the directions.** Exactly two answers are required. A third is worth at most $40\%$ of its marks, so time spent on it is worth less than half of time spent improving the two — and answering only one leaves marks on the table that nothing can recover.

Then: that $\gcd \times \mathrm{lcm} = ab$, which turns the given product into $ab$ and lets you divide out $a$. Compute $a$ first — $1^1+2^2+3^3 = 1+4+27 = 32 = 2^5$, so $a = 2^5\times 13$ — and the factorisation of $b$ falls out. The condition $b \equiv 0 \pmod 2$ is there to settle an ambiguity, so use it.

The second part is a coprimality question: exhibit $x,y$ with $(a-1)x + (b-1)y = 1$, or run the Euclidean algorithm.

- [Practice Assignment 8, Exercise 26](#PA08-NumbersAIO_ex26) — finding one of gcd/lcm from the product, by subtracting exponents.
- [Exercise 25](#PA08-NumbersAIO_ex25), [Exercise 27](#PA08-NumbersAIO_ex27) — the identity and its proof.
- [Exercise 45](#PA08-NumbersAIO_ex45) — showing two expressions are relatively prime, by Bézout and by repeated subtraction.
- [Greatest common divisor](#CONCEPT_greatest-common-divisor), [Bézout's theorem](#CONCEPT_bezout-theorem).

- **Choose two, and say which two.** Mark them clearly.
- $a$ evaluated and factorised before anything else.
- The identity **named** when it is used, not merely applied.
- Every exponent subtracted prime by prime, including the primes appearing in only one place.
- For the coprimality part, a **check line**: multiply your $x,y$ back out and confirm you get $1$.

- **Answering all three carefully.** The third is capped at $40\%$ bonus; the arithmetic on how to spend the time is part of the exam.
- **Multiplying instead of dividing.** $\mathrm{lcm} = ab/\gcd$.
- **Ignoring $b \equiv 0 \pmod 2$.** It is given because it is needed.
- **Answering "coprime" with no witnesses.** Produce $x$ and $y$, or the algorithm.

sections:
Determine whether

$$\Big[\exists x\,\big(P(x)\wedge \exists y\, Q(x,y)\big)\Big] \;\vee\; \Big[\forall y\,\forall x\,\big(Q(y,x)\rightarrow \neg P(y)\big)\Big]$$

is **valid** in first-order predicate logic. Explain all your steps.

*Asked in the MET midterms of WS24 and `64_XM_MT_DM`.*

The difference between **valid** and **true**, which is the whole point of the word. A first-order expression is *valid* when it comes out true under **every** interpretation — every universe, every meaning of the predicates. It is not enough that you cannot think of a counterexample.

The structure is a disjunction of two halves, and the second looks very like the negation of the first. If the two halves are genuine negations of each other, the disjunction is $S \vee \neg S$ and valid by excluded middle. So the work is: negate the first half properly, and compare.

$$\neg\exists x\,\big(P(x)\wedge\exists y\,Q(x,y)\big) \;\equiv\; \forall x\,\forall y\,\big(P(x)\to\neg Q(x,y)\big)$$

Then read the second half carefully — the argument order in $Q(y,x)$ and the bound-variable names are exactly where this question is won or lost.

- [Practice Assignment 3, Exercise 17](#PA03-FoL-AIO_ex17) onwards — validity, and interpretations as counterexamples.
- [Exercise 3](#PA03-FoL-AIO_ex3), [Exercise 5](#PA03-FoL-AIO_ex5), [Exercise 6](#PA03-FoL-AIO_ex6) — negating quantified statements.
- [Validity in predicate logic](#CONCEPT_validity-in-fol); [Nested quantifiers](#CONCEPT_quantifier-nesting) for what the variable order does.

- The negation pushed inward one quantifier at a time, each flip shown.
- An explicit comparison of the second half with that negation, **including the argument order of $Q$**.
- If valid: say which tautology it reduces to, and why the reduction is legitimate.
- If not valid: give an **interpretation** — universe, predicates, evaluation — under which it fails. That is the only counterexample available; there is no truth table in predicate logic.

- **Testing one interpretation and concluding "valid".** One interpretation shows *satisfiable*, never valid.
- **Ignoring the argument order.** $Q(x,y)$ and $Q(y,x)$ are different, and renaming bound variables does not fix a swap.
- **Flipping only the outer quantifier when negating.**
- **Omitting the evaluation** in a counter-interpretation.

sections:
Prove or disprove each of about seven statements, among them *"the sum of any 5 consecutive integers is divisible by 5"*, *"if $k^3$ is even then $k$ is even"*, *"$\sqrt[3]{2}$ is not rational"*, *"$n$ is odd if and only if $n$ is the sum of two consecutive integers"*, and *"$m^2+m$ is even"*.

The same permission line applies:

> *"You may directly apply theorems without proving them if they have already been proven in the lectures, but not if they were only covered in the practice assignments."*

*The MET counterpart of the BI list in [Midterm WS24 (BI), Question 5](#EXAM_64_WS24_MT_ex5); four statements overlap and three differ.*

Method selection across a spread of shapes, and in this list each of the four main methods is needed at least once:

| statement | the method it wants |
|---|---|
| sum of 5 consecutive integers | **direct** — write them as $n, n+1, \ldots, n+4$ and add |
| $k^3$ even $\to$ $k$ even | **contraposition** — assume $k$ odd, cube it |
| $\sqrt[3]{2}$ is irrational | **contradiction** — assume $p/q$ in lowest terms |
| $m^2+m$ is even | **cases**, or factor as $m(m+1)$ |
| the biconditional | **two directions**, labelled |

Recognising which is which, fast, is the skill being marked.

- Practice Assignment 4 throughout — all four methods.
- [Practice Assignment 8, Exercise 18](#PA08-NumbersAIO_ex18) — parity by cases.
- [Exercise 23](#PA08-NumbersAIO_ex23) — contraposition chosen because the direct route gives nothing to hold.
- [Exercise 38](#PA08-NumbersAIO_ex38) — a contradiction proof set out in full.
- [Proof by contradiction](#CONCEPT_proof-by-contradiction), [Proof by cases](#CONCEPT_proof-by-cases), [Proof by contraposition](#CONCEPT_proof-by-contraposition).

- The method named before each part begins.
- For $\sqrt[3]{2}$: the **lowest terms** assumption stated, and the contradiction named when it arrives.
- For $m^2+m$: either both parity cases, or the observation that $m(m+1)$ is a product of consecutive integers — and then a sentence saying why one of them must be even.
- Both directions of the biconditional.
- Only lecture theorems cited.

- **Assuming $k$ even and cubing.** That proves the converse. Contraposition assumes $k$ **odd**.
- **A contradiction proof that never uses the assumption.** If you never invoke $\neg S$, you gave a direct proof with extra words.
- **Forgetting "in lowest terms".** Without it the $\sqrt[3]{2}$ argument has no contradiction to reach.
- **Citing a practice-assignment result.** Forbidden in writing on this paper.

sections:
Let $A$, $B$, $C$ be propositional letters. **Without using truth tables**, determine whether

$$A \to (B \to \neg C) \;\equiv\; C \to (A \to \neg B)$$

Justify your decision by detailing your steps.

*This question appeared in both the MET and BI midterms of WS24, and again in the `64_XM_MT_DM` papers — four chunks, one question.*

Whether you can run a **chain of named equivalences** rather than reach for a truth table. The words "without using truth tables" are not a suggestion — they fix the method, and the material warns that in 99% of cases a valid argument must be shown by formal proof rather than by table.

Underneath, it is testing one rewrite: **implication**, $p \to q \equiv \neg p \vee q$. Once both sides are pushed into $\vee$ and $\neg$ form, the comparison is mechanical.

- The method named in the first line, and no truth table anywhere.
- **Every step justified by name** — "by IMP", "by De Morgan", "by commutativity". A chain of unnamed rewrites is an assertion, not a proof.
- A verdict stated plainly at the end, not left for the reader to infer.
- If the two sides turn out **not** to be equivalent, one truth assignment making them differ is the whole disproof — and that single row is not a truth table.

- **Building the truth table anyway.** Eight rows, correctly computed, against an instruction not to. It earns nothing.
- **Rewriting one side only and stopping when it "looks like" the other.** Take both to the same normal form.
- **Confusing the rewrite with the converse.** $A \to (B\to\neg C)$ is not $(B \to \neg C)\to A$.
- **Skipping the verdict.** State it, in capitals.

sections:
Determine whether

$$\neg\Big[\exists x\,\big(P(x)\wedge \exists y\, Q(y)\big)\Big] \qquad\text{and}\qquad \Big[\forall y\,\forall x\,\big(P(y)\rightarrow \neg Q(x)\big)\Big]$$

are logically equivalent in first-order predicate logic. Explain all your steps.

*Asked in both the WS24 and `64_XM_MT_DM` BI midterms.*

Pushing a negation through **nested quantifiers**, one at a time, flipping each — and then recognising the propositional rewrite underneath.

The two moves that do the work:

$$\neg\exists x\, S(x) \equiv \forall x\, \neg S(x) \qquad\text{and}\qquad \neg(p \wedge q) \equiv \neg p \vee \neg q \equiv p \to \neg q$$

Note also that the two formulas use the bound variables in **opposite** roles — $P(x)$ against $P(y)$ — so part of the question is whether you notice that a bound variable's name carries no meaning.

- [Practice Assignment 3, Exercise 3](#PA03-FoL-AIO_ex3), [Exercise 5](#PA03-FoL-AIO_ex5), [Exercise 6](#PA03-FoL-AIO_ex6) — negating quantified statements step by step.
- [Exercise 10](#PA03-FoL-AIO_ex10), [Exercise 15](#PA03-FoL-AIO_ex15), [Exercise 22](#PA03-FoL-AIO_ex22) — nested quantifiers.
- [Nested quantifiers](#CONCEPT_quantifier-nesting) for the order rules; [Variables and quantification](#CONCEPT_variables-and-quantification) for the negation rules.

- The negation pushed inward **one quantifier at a time**, each flip visible. Do not jump to the answer.
- Each propositional step named.
- An explicit statement about the **renaming of bound variables**, if you rename them — it is legitimate and it must be said.
- A verdict.

"Explain all your steps" is in the question. In real tests students must explicitly include all required information.

- **Flipping only the outer quantifier.** $\neg\exists x\exists y$ becomes $\forall x \forall y$ — both.
- **Treating $x$ and $y$ as different objects because they have different letters.** A bound variable's name is arbitrary.
- **Negating $\wedge$ into $\wedge$.** De Morgan turns it into $\vee$, which then becomes the conditional.
- **Answering with a truth table.** There is none for predicate logic; an interpretation is the only counterexample available.

sections:
Describe a domain of interpretation $\mathcal{I}_1$ under which

$$\forall x\,\Big(\big[P(x)\vee\neg Q(x)\big] \longrightarrow \exists y\, R(x,y)\Big)$$

is **False**, and a domain $\mathcal{I}_2$ under which the same expression is **True**.

In each case your answer must specify the universe, what each predicate denotes, and how the expression is evaluated under the interpretation.

*Asked in the WS24 and `64_XM_MT_DM` midterms, MET and BI — four chunks, one question.*

That you can build an **interpretation**, which is the predicate-logic counterpart of a truth assignment: a universe, plus a meaning for every predicate on it. This is the only way to disprove a claim in first-order logic — there is no truth table.

The formula is a universal over a conditional, so:

- to make it **False**, you need **one** $x$ satisfying the antecedent and having **no** $y$ with $R(x,y)$;
- to make it **True**, the cheapest routes are to make the antecedent fail everywhere, or to make $\exists y\,R(x,y)$ hold everywhere.

- [Practice Assignment 3, Exercise 17](#PA03-FoL-AIO_ex17) onwards — validity and counter-interpretations.
- [Practice Assignment 2, Exercise 6](#PA02-Inferences_ex6) — a predicate-logic argument worked in full with a stated domain.
- [Validity in predicate logic](#CONCEPT_validity-in-fol) sets out what an interpretation must contain and why a tiny universe is usually the right choice.

- **Giving the universe and predicates but not evaluating.** An unevaluated interpretation is a guess.
- **Choosing a large or infinite universe.** $\{1,2\}$ is easier to check and just as valid.
- **Making the antecedent false to get $\mathcal{I}_1$.** A false antecedent makes the conditional **true**. For the False case the antecedent must **hold** and the consequent fail.
- **Forgetting that $R$ is binary.** $R(x,y)$ needs a value for every pair.

Over the universe $\mathbb{Z}$, and using **only** the predicates supplied — `Prime`, `Odd`, `Even`, `Positive`, `Square(n,m)`, `Greater(n,m)`, `Equals(n,m)`, `Times(n,m,p)` — and the constant `TWO`, express a list of English statements in first-order predicate logic, using appropriate quantifiers.

*Asked in the MET and BI midterms of WS24 and again in `64_XM_MT_DM` — four chunks, one question.*

Translation under a **fixed vocabulary**. The universe and the dictionary are given, so the marks are entirely in choosing the quantifiers and the connective correctly, and in **not reaching for anything not on the list** — no $+$, no $\times$, no $<$, only `Times` and `Greater`.

The two shapes that decide most of it:

- a universal claim takes a **conditional**: $\forall x\,(P(x) \to Q(x))$;
- an existential claim takes a **conjunction**: $\exists x\,(P(x) \wedge Q(x))$.

Writing $\exists x\,(P(x)\to Q(x))$ is the classic error — it is true whenever anything at all fails $P$.

- [Practice Assignment 3, Exercise 1](#PA03-FoL-AIO_ex1) to [Exercise 12](#PA03-FoL-AIO_ex12) — translation with the domain stated, and both shapes side by side.
- [Exercise 10](#PA03-FoL-AIO_ex10), [Exercise 15](#PA03-FoL-AIO_ex15), [Exercise 22](#PA03-FoL-AIO_ex22) — nested quantifiers.
- [Translating English into logic](#CONCEPT_translation-to-logic) for the English-to-symbol table; [Nested quantifiers](#CONCEPT_quantifier-nesting) for the order.

- **Only the supplied predicates.** Using arithmetic notation the list does not provide is the fastest way to lose a part you had right.
- The quantifier and the connective matched to the shape of the sentence.
- For a relational predicate, the **argument order** as defined: `Greater(n,m)` is "$n$ is greater than $m$", not the reverse.
- Where a statement needs a constant, use `TWO` rather than the numeral.

- **$\to$ with $\exists$, or $\wedge$ with $\forall$.** The single most costly slip in the whole topic.
- **Reversing the arguments of a two-place predicate.**
- **Inventing a predicate.** If the list has no `LessThan`, express it with `Greater` and swapped arguments.
- **Leaving a variable free.** Every variable must be bound; an unbound one means the translation is not a proposition — and in this course that is not a technicality.

sections:
Prove or disprove each of about seven statements — among them *"if the product of three integers is odd then at least two are even"*, *"if $n^2-6n+5$ is even then $n$ is odd"*, *"$n(n+1)/2$ is an integer"*, *"$n$ is odd if and only if $n$ is the sum of two consecutive integers"*, and *"if $n>51$ is odd then $n!$ is odd"*.

The paper carries an explicit permission, and it is worth quoting exactly:

> *"You may directly apply theorems without proving them if they have already been proven in the lectures, but not if they were only covered in the practice assignments."*

*Asked in the WS24 midterm in both MET and BI versions, with the list differing slightly between them.*

**Choosing the method**, seven times over, quickly. Each statement is short, and the whole question is decided by whether you spot which of these it wants:

| the statement | the move |
|---|---|
| a universal claim that is false | **one counterexample**, and stop |
| a conditional with an awkward hypothesis | **contraposition** |
| an "if and only if" | **two proofs**, labelled |
| a claim about every integer, split by parity | **cases** |

And it is testing that you read the permission line. A theorem from the lectures may be cited; the same result from a practice assignment may **not** — you must prove it.

- Practice Assignment 4 throughout — direct, contraposition, contradiction, cases.
- [Practice Assignment 8, Exercise 18](#PA08-NumbersAIO_ex18) — the parity-cases pattern, for the $m^2+m$ and $n(n+1)/2$ statements.
- [Exercise 7](#PA08-NumbersAIO_ex7), [Exercise 13](#PA08-NumbersAIO_ex13), [Exercise 17](#PA08-NumbersAIO_ex17) — counterexamples, and how to present one.
- [Theorems and proofs](#CONCEPT_theorems-and-proofs), [Counterexamples](#CONCEPT_counterexamples), [Proof by contraposition](#CONCEPT_proof-by-contraposition).

- **Decide first.** Test two or three small cases before committing; that is not part of the answer, it is how you avoid an hour proving something false.
- **Name the method** in the first line of each part.
- A counterexample states the values, evaluates the hypothesis, evaluates the conclusion, and says the claim is disproved. All four.
- A biconditional gets **both** directions, each labelled.
- **Cite only lecture theorems.** If you use a result, say where it came from.

- **Giving examples for a true universal claim.** Do not give an example, or a million examples, when the required proof contains a universal generalization.
- **Citing a practice-assignment result.** The question forbids it in writing.
- **Proving one direction of an "if and only if".**
- **Trying to prove a false statement** because you did not test it first.

sections:
Five pharaohs — AbuSimbel, Bocchoris, Cheops, Djoser, Eratosthenes — each either building a pyramid or not. Four premises are given, including *"Bocchoris is building if and only if AbuSimbel is not"* and *"it is not true that Cheops is building or Djoser is building"*.

Deduce who is building and who is not, write the full symbolic form of the argument, and **justify it with a formal proof sequence**.

The paper states its own rule, and it is stricter than you may expect:

> *"You are only allowed to use equivalence rules or the listed inference rules in the formula sheet. You are not allowed to use an unlisted inference rule, even if you proved it."*

*Asked in the WS24 and `64_XM_MT_DM` BI midterms.*

The whole propositional-logic chapter at once: translation, then a **derivation** with every line justified. The puzzle is a knights-and-knaves problem in exam clothing.

The premises are chosen so that one of them collapses immediately: *"not ($C$ or $D$)"* is De Morgan into $\neg C \wedge \neg D$, which gives two atoms outright. From there the biconditionals fall.

- [Practice Assignment 1, Exercise 23](#PA01-PL_ex23), [Exercise 24](#PA01-PL_ex24), [Exercise 32](#PA01-PL_ex32) — the knights-and-knaves pattern, case by case and by negation.
- [Practice Assignment 2, Exercise 3](#PA02-Inferences_ex3) and [Exercise 10](#PA02-Inferences_ex10) — derivations laid out in the course's own three-column table.
- [Derivations](#CONCEPT_derivations) and [Proof sequences](#CONCEPT_proof-sequences) for the layout and the self-check.

- The **dictionary** first: $A$ denotes "AbuSimbel is building", and so on.
- The premises in symbols, each labelled to match the question's $\langle T_1\rangle$, $\langle F_1\rangle$ tags.
- A numbered proof sequence: proposition, then a justification naming **the rule and the line numbers**.
- A conclusion naming, for every one of the five, whether they build.
- Disjunctions in the premises read as **inclusive**, as the question says — even though the build/not-build choice itself is exclusive.

- **Using an inference rule that is not on the formula sheet.** This paper bans it *even if you proved it* — stricter than the general course rule, and it is written on the paper. Equivalence rules stay unrestricted.
- **Reasoning in English and calling it a proof sequence.** The question asks for the symbolic form and the numbered derivation.
- **Applying a rule to part of a line.** Rules apply to whole lines; simplify first.
- **Answering the puzzle without the derivation.** The right five answers with no proof is not what was asked.
